newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin due back at suburban Moscow home on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin due back at suburban Moscow home on Sunday.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was scheduled to return to his suburban Moscow home on Sunday, a day before his planned return to work in the Kremlin, his spokesman said.
Since undergoing heart surgery last month, the president has slowly resumed working and meeting top officials during his recovery, but has not visited the Kremlin.

Yeltsin had multiple heart bypass operation on November 5, and has stayed in several residences outside Moscow since then. On Sunday, he is due to return to his home in Gorky-9, a wooded area 20 km (12 miles) from the capital.
On Saturday, the president started working at the Rus residence about 100 km (60 miles) outside Moscow at 6.30 a.m., his press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said.

As Yeltsin planned to move closer to the Kremlin, Russian voters in 15 of the country's 89 regions on Sunday were casting ballots in gubernatorial and other local elections. A series of Communists and other opposition candidates are challenging politicians supported by the government.
Russians in the country's Far East, Siberia and the Volga region -- including oil-rich Tyumen and diamond-producer Sakha, formerly Yakutia -- were among those going to the polls.
The elections are important not only for their regional impact, but also because Russian governors serve in the upper house of parliament, the Federation Council.

On Saturday, the Kremlin press office attemped to highlight the president's return by granting Reuters Television and Russian stations a rare tour of his office, lined with wood panelling and bookcases, and illuminated by two ornate chandeliers.
It is to these elegant surroundings that Yeltsin, speaking on Friday in his first television interview since his operation, said he was anxious to return.

"I feel that the recovery period is over. I am returning to the Kremlin on Monday...I will be there at nine a.m. The doctors have done their job and now it is up to the president," he told the nation.
"The country needs an active and energetic president, especially now," he said.
Yeltsin, who appeared to have lost weight since his surgery, spoke in a firm and decisive voice throughout the interview, though he appeared to be moving stiffly.
Among the problems Yeltsin said he was anxious to address were workers' unpaid wages, the peace process in the breakaway region of Chechnya and reform of the army and military doctrine.

In his remarks on Friday, the president also warned he would crack the whip over government officials who have not worked hard enough in his absence, and said business managers who do not pay taxes should lose their jobs.
The president's first order of business on Monday morning will be meeting top aides and government officials, Yastrzembsky said.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was expected to fly to Tehran on Sunday for two days of talks with his Iranian counterpart, the Foreign Ministry said.
